heuristics.rule: If your Canadian master's program is 2+ years, you get a 3-year PGWP; if it's 1 year, you get a 1-year PGWP — the program length decision is effectively an immigration decision.
heuristics.condition: When an international student is selecting between a 1-year and 2-year Canadian master's program...
heuristics.action: ...treat the extra year of study as purchasing 2 additional years of open work authorization, not just an academic upgrade
heuristics.because: A 3-year PGWP creates enough runway to accumulate 1 year of skilled work experience, apply for CEC, and receive PR before the permit expires — a 1-year PGWP does not

heuristics.rule: During PGWP, tell employers 'I have open work authorization — no sponsorship required' rather than disclosing visa status framing
heuristics.condition: When a PGWP holder is in job search mode and an employer asks about work authorization...
heuristics.action: ...frame it as 'I have a 3-year open work permit valid until [date], no sponsorship required,' and proactively mention the PR pathway
heuristics.because: PGWP is legally equivalent to domestic work authorization for employers — framing it as a 'visa issue' creates false hesitation that doesn't exist

heuristics.rule: If a tech role qualifies for Global Talent Stream Category B, tell employers the sponsorship burden is 2 weeks, not months
heuristics.condition: When negotiating post-PGWP work authorization with a tech employer who is unfamiliar with GTS...
heuristics.action: ...explicitly state that GTS processing takes 2 weeks and requires no LMIA for eligible occupations, and name the category
heuristics.because: Employer hesitation about post-PGWP sponsorship is often based on conflating it with normal LMIA (3-6 months); GTS removes the objection entirely for eligible roles

heuristics.rule: After 1 year of skilled Canadian work, frame your retention story to employers as 'I'll have PR in 2-3 years' — not 'I'm on a visa'
heuristics.condition: When an employer raises concerns about long-term retention of a PGWP worker...
heuristics.action: ...explain the CEC → Express Entry → PR pathway with concrete timelines, positioning PR as near-certain rather than contingent
heuristics.because: Unlike H-1B lottery (binary annual event with ~20% odds), CEC/Express Entry is rolling and deterministic once work experience is accumulated — the uncertainty level is fundamentally different

heuristics.rule: If your long-term goal is Canadian PR, optimize job search by province PNP eligibility, not just salary
heuristics.condition: When a PGWP holder has job offers in multiple provinces or is targeting job search geographically...
heuristics.action: ...evaluate each offer's PR pathway speed via provincial PNP streams (BC Tech Pilot, OINP, SINP) alongside compensation
heuristics.because: A PNP nomination can add 600 CRS points, essentially guaranteeing an ITA — a lower-paying job in a PNP-accessible province may yield PR years faster than a higher-paying offer in a competitive province

heuristics.rule: Never accept 'LMIA pending' as a hiring condition unless you have verified the employer has successfully completed an LMIA before
heuristics.condition: When an employer makes a job offer contingent on LMIA approval...
heuristics.action: ...ask for evidence of prior successful LMIA completions and understand that LMIA is the employer's cost and responsibility — you should pay nothing
heuristics.because: LMIA processing takes months and can be denied; unverified employers may be unfamiliar with the process, leaving you in limbo or unemployed after turning down other offers

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether PR can be obtained before open work authorization expires — a 1-year PGWP creates a dangerous gap window; a 3-year PGWP provides enough runway for CEC eligibility and PR processing
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate: program length → PGWP duration → subtract 1 year to CEC eligibility → add 6-12 months for PR processing → compare to PGWP expiry date

decision_factors.factor: Role eligibility for Global Talent Stream Category B
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines post-PGWP employer sponsorship burden — GTS Category B reduces it to 2 weeks vs. 3-6 months for standard LMIA, making employer willingness to sponsor dramatically higher
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check if your NOC code appears on the Global Talent Occupations List published by ESDC; confirm role matches the listed occupation description

decision_factors.factor: Province of job offer relative to PNP stream eligibility
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Provincial nomination can add 600 CRS points, essentially guaranteeing PR invitation — the province of employment determines which PNP streams are accessible
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check BC Tech Pilot, OINP Masters Graduate stream, AAIP, and SINP eligibility criteria against your NOC code, education, and job offer details; compare processing times across provinces

decision_factors.why_it_matters: French proficiency adds 25-50 CRS points — in competitive Express Entry draws where margins are small, this can be the difference between receiving an ITA or not
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Evaluate current French ability honestly; calculate potential CRS score increase from TEF/TCF scores using the IRCC CRS calculator

decision_factors.why_it_matters: CEC requires 'employed' work experience — contractor/self-employment income does not qualify, meaning misclassification can silently invalidate PR eligibility accumulation
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Review offer letter classification; confirm T4 employment (not T4A contractor) will be issued; verify the company has an employer CRA account number

decision_factors.factor: Employer's prior LMIA or GTS sponsorship track record
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Employers with no prior sponsorship experience frequently underestimate complexity, timeline, and cost — offers contingent on novel LMIA processes carry high failure risk
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask directly whether the company has sponsored foreign workers before; ask for the name of their immigration law firm; search job postings for prior LMIA-backed roles

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Language scores are a directly controllable CRS input — higher scores translate directly to more CRS points and faster PR, unlike age or work experience which are fixed
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Use IRCC CRS calculator to simulate score impact; compare current score to CLB 9-10 benchmarks and calculate point gain from improvement

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a higher-paying job offer in Ontario over a lower-paying offer in Saskatchewan
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Ontario's competitive OINP pool and higher CRS cut-off scores may delay PR by 2-4 years compared to a Saskatchewan PNP stream where selection is less competitive
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PGWP holders with moderate CRS scores (below 470-480) who would not rank highly in federal Express Entry draws but might qualify for provincial streams

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking a 1-year master's program to save tuition and time
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: 1-year PGWP means you must find a job, accumulate 1 year of CEC-eligible work experience, apply, and receive PR — all before the PGWP expires — leaving almost no margin for job search delays, unemployment gaps, or processing backlogs
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who don't model out the post-graduation immigration timeline before selecting their program

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting contractor classification from an employer to get hired faster or at higher pay
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Self-employment income does not count toward the 1 year of skilled work required for Canadian Experience Class, silently delaying or invalidating your PR eligibility accumulation
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Tech workers and consultants who are offered contractor arrangements, which are common in Canadian tech hiring

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying solely on federal Express Entry without exploring PNP streams
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Federal Express Entry CRS cut-offs fluctuate and can be unpredictably high — exclusive reliance on it creates timeline uncertainty that provincial nomination would eliminate for eligible candidates
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PGWP holders approaching PGWP expiry who assumed Express Entry was straightforward and did not build PNP eligibility into their job targeting strategy

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an 'unpaid internship for Canadian experience'
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Unpaid internships are illegal under Employment Standards Act for most workers in Canada — the experience may not be defensible as legitimate employment, and the worker is being exploited based on perceived visa vulnerability
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Recent graduates with short PGWP durations who feel pressure to build Canadian work history quickly and don't know their legal protections

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating Canadian job search like US job search by filtering employers for 'sponsorship willingness' during PGWP period
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: International students with US exposure or who read US-focused immigration advice apply the same sponsor-filter logic to Canada, not realizing PGWP is open work authorization requiring no employer action
failure_patterns.consequence: Self-selection out of large portions of the job market that would have hired them freely, unnecessarily lengthening job search and limiting options
warning_signs: Spending time researching which Canadian companies 'sponsor visas' before applying
Avoiding small and mid-size employers because 'they won't sponsor'

failure_patterns.pattern: Not modeling the PR timeline against PGWP expiry date before accepting a program or job
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students optimize for short-term factors (lower tuition, faster graduation, higher salary) without calculating whether the resulting PGWP duration provides enough runway for PR before expiry
failure_patterns.consequence: Ending up in LMIA dependency before achieving PR, with all the attendant risks of employer-tied immigration status
warning_signs: Choosing a 1-year master's program without calculating post-graduation immigration runway
Accepting a job offer without asking whether it creates CEC-eligible work experience in time

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting contractor classification from employer without understanding CEC implications
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Contractor arrangements are presented as standard or advantageous (higher hourly rate), and the worker doesn't know that CEC requires T4 employment rather than T4A contractor income
failure_patterns.consequence: Months or years of Canadian work experience that don't count toward CEC eligibility, discovered only when applying for PR
warning_signs: Offer letter says 'independent contractor' or 'consulting agreement'
Employer says they will issue a T4A rather than a T4

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting 'LMIA pending' offers from employers without prior sponsorship experience
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates are relieved to have an offer and don't investigate whether the employer has operational knowledge of LMIA processing; employers sometimes make offers in good faith without understanding the complexity
failure_patterns.consequence: Months of waiting, possible LMIA denial, and having declined other offers in the interim — potential gap in status if PGWP expires during the wait
warning_signs: Employer cannot name their immigration law firm
Employer is unclear about LMIA cost and processing timeline when asked directly

failure_patterns.pattern: Not learning French despite clear, calculable CRS point gain
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates underestimate how competitive Express Entry draws can be and don't model the specific CRS point value of French proficiency improvement
failure_patterns.consequence: Missing PR invitations by small margins that French language points would have covered, extending the timeline by months or years
warning_signs: Candidate knows French is 'helpful' but has not calculated their exact CRS score gap
Candidate dismisses French study as 'too hard' without evaluating the PR timeline cost of not pursuing it

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the exact expiry date of your PGWP, and have you calculated whether you can receive PR before that date?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate has a workable immigration runway or is already in a high-risk timeline squeeze
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is your CEC eligibility date, and what is your current CRS score estimate — have you modeled whether that score is competitive in current draws?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Calculate immediately: PGWP expiry minus 18 months (1 year CEC accumulation + 6 months PR processing) = your hard deadline for starting a CEC-eligible job

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your current or target job classified as T4 employment or T4A contractor?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the work experience being accumulated will count toward the 1-year CEC requirement for PR eligibility
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Confirm the employer has a CRA payroll account and that you are listed as an employee on their records
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Understand that contractor income does not count toward CEC — evaluate whether renegotiating classification or switching employers is necessary

diagnostic_questions.question: Does your NOC code appear on the Global Talent Occupations List?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether post-PGWP employer sponsorship can be framed as a 2-week GTS process rather than a months-long LMIA — changes the employer conversation entirely
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Prepare a one-paragraph explanation of GTS Category B to share with HR if post-PGWP sponsorship concerns arise
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Identify whether a Category A GTS referral through a designated partner organization could apply, or plan around LMIA timeline risks

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you researched the PNP streams for the province where you are targeting jobs, and does your profile meet their eligibility criteria?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate is optimizing for PR speed or defaulting to federal Express Entry without considering faster provincial pathways
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Quantify the CRS advantage of a PNP nomination (typically +600 points) and assess whether geographic targeting changes are worth making
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Research BC Tech Pilot, OINP Masters Graduate stream, and SINP occupation lists before finalizing geographic job search strategy

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your current estimated CRS score, and what is the gap between your score and recent Express Entry cut-off scores for your eligible program?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate is realistically competitive in federal Express Entry or needs a PNP pathway, language improvement, or job offer to close the gap
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Identify which CRS factors are improvable (language scores, French proficiency, job offer) and model the score impact of each
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Use IRCC's official CRS calculator to establish a baseline score before making any decisions about job targeting, province selection, or timeline planning

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have any French language ability, and have you calculated the CRS point impact of achieving a TEF/TCF score?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate is leaving a directly controllable and potentially decisive CRS lever unused
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Calculate exact CRS score increase from current to B2/C1 French and compare the time investment to the PR timeline improvement it would yield
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Assess French language baseline — even moderate French (CLB 7-9) can add 25-50 CRS points, which may be the margin between receiving an ITA or not

industry_realities.common_belief: International students in Canada face the same employer sponsorship barriers as in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: PGWP holders have open work authorization — employers do not need to sponsor, file paperwork, or pay legal fees during the PGWP period. The barrier simply does not exist for the first 1-3 years.
industry_realities.implication: PGWP holders should conduct job searches identically to domestic candidates — no sponsor-filter, no avoidance of small employers, no pre-screening for 'visa friendliness'

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting PR in Canada is uncertain and lottery-like, similar to the H-1B in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: For someone with 1 year of skilled Canadian work experience, CEC/Express Entry is deterministic and rolling — it is not a lottery. CRS scores can be calculated, gaps can be addressed, and PNP streams can add 600 points to make selection near-certain.
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should present their PR pathway to employers as a credible, near-certain outcome with a concrete timeline, not as an uncertain future contingency

industry_realities.common_belief: An LMIA means an employer cannot or will not hire a foreign worker for that role
industry_realities.actual_reality: LMIA is a process employers use to hire foreign workers — it is a mechanism that enables hiring, not a barrier. For tech roles, Global Talent Stream reduces this to a 2-week process.
industry_realities.implication: Post-PGWP candidates in tech should proactively educate employers about GTS rather than assuming LMIA requirements will end the conversation

industry_realities.common_belief: The best province for a job offer is Ontario or BC because of their large tech markets
industry_realities.actual_reality: Ontario and BC have the most competitive PNP streams and highest CRS cut-offs. Provinces like Saskatchewan may offer faster PR pathways for the same NOC code through less competitive streams.
industry_realities.implication: Candidates optimizing for PR speed should weight provincial PNP accessibility alongside salary and market size when evaluating geographic job search strategy

industry_realities.common_belief: Unpaid internships are a legitimate way to build Canadian work experience when you can't find paid work
industry_realities.actual_reality: Unpaid internships are illegal for most workers under provincial Employment Standards Acts. Employers offering them to international graduates are exploiting perceived visa vulnerability, not providing a legal or credible pathway.
industry_realities.implication: International graduates should refuse unpaid internships and understand that accepting one neither builds legitimate CEC-eligible experience nor is legally required of them

industry_realities.common_belief: Contractor arrangements pay more and offer flexibility — they are an equivalent or better option for building Canadian work experience
industry_realities.actual_reality: CEC requires employed (T4) work experience. Independent contractor income (T4A) does not count toward the 1-year skilled work requirement. Contractor classification can silently void months of intended PR eligibility accumulation.
industry_realities.implication: International workers should insist on T4 employment classification and treat contractor offers as a PR eligibility risk, not just a tax consideration

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Understanding of PGWP as work authorization
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats PGWP as 'a visa that needs to be explained' to employers and pre-filters companies based on assumed sponsorship willingness
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: States 'I have open work authorization' confidently, makes no distinction from domestic candidates during PGWP period, and only discusses immigration when the post-PGWP timeline is a legitimate employer concern
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Junior framing creates friction and hesitation that doesn't legally exist; senior framing removes it and focuses the conversation on the job

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Thinks about PR as something to figure out 'later' or assumes Express Entry will work out when the time comes
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Models the full immigration timeline on day one: PGWP expiry → CEC eligibility date → CRS score estimate → PNP eligibility → ITA probability → chooses employer, province, and role classification accordingly
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Failure to model the timeline early leads to discovering eligibility gaps only when it's too late to correct them without status gaps

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Evaluates offers on compensation and role quality; treats immigration implications (contractor vs. employee, province, NOC code) as secondary or irrelevant
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Evaluates offers on compensation, role quality, AND PR pathway implications — NOC code eligibility, employment vs. contractor classification, provincial PNP access, and employer's prior sponsorship track record
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A higher-paying contractor offer in Ontario may yield PR 3 years later than a lower-paying employee offer in Saskatchewan — the financial calculus reverses when PR timeline is included

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Responding to post-PGWP sponsorship concern from employers
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Becomes defensive or vague about immigration status when employer raises post-PGWP concerns; treats it as a dealbreaker signal
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Proactively prepares a one-paragraph GTS explanation for tech roles, names the specific stream, quotes the 2-week processing time, and frames the conversation as 'here is why this is not a burden for your company'
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Employer hesitation about immigration is usually based on conflating all work permit processes with the worst-case LMIA scenario — a knowledgeable candidate can dissolve the objection in one conversation

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Targets Toronto or Vancouver because that is 'where the tech jobs are' without assessing provincial PNP eligibility
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Maps target NOC codes against all provincial PNP streams, compares estimated CRS scores to recent cut-off data, and builds geographic flexibility into job search based on PR pathway speed, not just market size
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The fastest PR path may not run through the most prestigious tech hub — seniors understand this tradeoff; juniors discover it after their PGWP is close to expiry

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Due diligence on employer immigration capability
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Accepts offer contingent on LMIA or sponsorship without verifying employer has prior experience completing the process
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Asks directly about prior LMIA completions, requests the name of the employer's immigration law firm, and treats inability to answer these questions as a significant offer risk signal
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: An employer's good faith intention to sponsor is worthless if they lack the operational knowledge to execute — the candidate bears the status risk if the process fails
